title: A rook crosses the boards twice and sets up mate
summary: White on board B won the queen in the fixed opening, but by move 20 the engine scored Black ahead there and White ahead on board A. The finish turns on one rook: White takes it with Bxg7 on board B, Black drops it on board A, gives it up there with Rxf2+ and Kxf2, and it returns to board B for R@h6+ before N@f6# mates. Watch Black on board A choose its last moves by what each would hand to Black on board B, where by the engine's count a single piece was enough to mate.
event: HypeBeast 1.1.1 against itself, 500,000 nodes a move for one team and 450,000 for the other

result.text: Black on board B mates; the team of A-White and B-Black wins.

moves.note: Bxd7+ gives the bishop for the pawn on d7: the pawn goes to Black on board A, the partner, and after Kxd7 the bishop goes to White there, who drops it with B@g2. Its first choice was Nf4. The engine switched because it gave nearly even chances that a knight would come from its partner, and with a knight in hand it liked Bxd7+ much better. No knight came, and White's score stayed about where it was.

lines.note: After Kxd7 the engine expected Qa4+, still scoring White about ten pawns down.
Its first choice, Nf4, answered by exf4.
A search that ignores the other board plays Qxg4; compared like for like, it scored about two pawns worse for White than Bxd7+.

moves.note: The pawn the engine had thought very likely to come from board B arrived when Black there played Qxf6, and White dropped a pawn on d2 at once. White already had three other pawns in hand, and its search rated P@d2 and P@f2 almost exactly the same. The engine scored the position about level.

lines.note: Black takes the pawn on d7, White the bishop on h4, and Black the bishop on e3 with check; about level by the engine's count.

moves.note: Its first choice was P@d3. The engine played P@d2 because it held up whatever came from board A: if a knight reached Black while White got a bishop, which it gave about one chance in five, it scored P@d3 about nineteen pawns down and P@d2 about level. What came was a pawn for White, through Qxd7 on board A, and P@d2 was its better move in that case too.

lines.note: The reply the engine expected; the game followed it with Rd1, P@c2 and Rxd2.
Its first choice, P@d3, answered by fxe4.
A search that ignores the other board plays h5; compared like for like, it scored about two pawns better for Black than P@d2.

moves.note: Its first choice, Q@e1+, wins the rook on h1, and with the bishop and knight that the trade on board A then delivered, the engine counted it as a forced mate. It played h5 expecting a pawn instead, but no pawn came: White dropped the arriving bishop with B@f8+ and took the rook on g7 with Bxg7, and Black's score fell from well ahead to a little behind. That rook comes back at the end for R@h6+.

lines.note: Had nothing arrived, the engine expected P@g5, still scoring Black about nine pawns up.
What White did with the bishop from board A: B@f8+, after which White's own search scored the game close to level.

moves.note: Its first choice was Kxf8. The engine played Ke8 in case a knight went to White, which it gave about one chance in three, and with that knight in White's hand it scored Kxf8 much worse. One did come, through Kxe7 on board A, and the bishop on f8 then took the rook on g7 with Bxg7.

Bxg7 takes the rook on g7 and sends it to Black on board A. Follow that rook: Black drops it with R@d2+, gives it up with Rxf2+, and after Kxf2 it comes back to this board for R@h6+, which sets up the mate.

Its first choice was R@c5, but if a bishop reached White here, which it gave about two chances in five, the engine scored that rook drop as losing, and by its count a rook for Black on board B was enough to mate there. P@f3 risks only a pawn, worth nothing to Black on board B by its count. The bishop came, with a queen for Black, from the captures on f3 on board B, and Black stayed well ahead. The rook stays in hand until R@d2+.

lines.note: White takes the pawn and Black checks with B@h3+; the engine scored this about nine and a half pawns for Black.
Its first choice: R@c5, and after gxh4, Rxc2.
A search that ignores the other board drops the rook on d2; compared like for like, it scored about three pawns worse for Black than P@f3.

moves.note: N@h4+ starts the king hunt that ends in mate: Kh3 is White's only reply, and the game follows the engine's line through P@g4+, Qxg4, hxg4+ and Kxg4. With a bishop or a pawn from board A the engine counted a forced mate, but neither came. Every other move it looked at was far worse by its count. Its score for Black changed sharply over the next few moves while the hunt went on.

lines.note: The engine's line, which the game followed for five moves.

moves.note: hxg4+ takes White's queen and sends it to White on board A, who was well behind there by the engine's quick look. Black on board A had scored itself about six pawns up just before this and about nine down just after.

White on board A had just received a queen from hxg4+ on board B. Its first choice was Q@e2, but the knight on f4 could take it with Nxe2, sending the queen to Black on board B, who could then mate with Q@f3. So it played Nxe3+, taking a pawn with check; by the engine's count even a bishop or a pawn for Black on board B was enough to mate there.

lines.note: White takes back, and the engine expected a rook check and an exchange on f2, scoring Black about eight pawns down.
Its first choice, Q@e2, ruled out because Nxe2 would hand the queen across.
With the expected pawn in hand the engine planned R@d2+ and an exchange on f2, close to what happened.

moves.note: This is the rook White on board B won with Bxg7, now dropped on board A. Its first choice was R@e2+, and a deeper look switched to R@d2+. On board A alone the engine scored Black far ahead, but the line of its first choice gave up a pawn and the bishop on h4, and by its count either piece was enough for Black on board B to mate, so it scored itself behind overall.

lines.note: White blocks with B@f2, and a fresh search scored this about level.
Its first choice, R@e2+, whose line gives up the pawn on d5 and the bishop on h4.
White's plan at its next turn, Q@f2, Rxf2+ and Kxf2, which is how the game went: Kxf2 sends the rook back to Black on board B.

moves.note: Qxe2+ gives the queen for the knight on e2, since the engine expected Rxe2: the knight goes to White on board A and the queen to Black there, and by its count the two nearly cancel. A single pawn from board A would have given it a forced mate, though it thought that unlikely. What came was the rook from Bxg7, through Rxf2+ and Kxf2 on board A, and Black used it at once with R@h6+.

lines.note: White takes the queen; the engine meant to go on checking with N@f4+, but the rook arrived first and it played R@h6+.

moves.note: Every move here handed Black on board B something, and by the engine's count a queen, a rook, a bishop or a pawn there was enough to mate. Its first choice, Q@g4, lost the queen to fxg4, and Black on board B could then mate with Q@g5, so it took White's queen with Rxf2+. White on board B got that queen but was mated before using it, while Kxf2 sent the rook to Black there for R@h6+. By its own count Black was lost whatever it played.

lines.note: Kxf2, and a fresh search still scored Black about twelve pawns down.
Its first choice, Q@g4, ruled out because fxg4 hands the queen to Black on board B.
The line it planned in case a queen came from board B, which it thought very likely, as one did with Rxe2.

moves.note: The rook from Kxf2 on board A, the one White took with Bxg7 long before, is dropped at once with check. Bxh6 is White's only move, and N@f6# mates: the engine counted mate in two.

lines.note: N@f4+ also mated in two by the engine's count, with the same rook.

moves.note: The queen came from Rxe2 on board B, as the engine had expected. With it Black on board A scored itself about sixteen pawns up, but board B was already lost: Black there had mate in two, and it came first.

lines.note: The engine's line, taking on e3 and e2 with checks.
With the rook it expected from board B, which came with Bxh6, it would have played the same queen check.

moves.note: N@f6# ends the game. On board A, White left the check from Q@d2+ unanswered and sat: its partner had mate in one, and while it sat Black there could capture nothing to send to White on board B. It had about a second and a half more on its clock than White on board B, more than it needed.
